q: Bottles sold for decades in California as Napa Gamay were made from a southern French variety called Valdiguie, and the authorities eventually withdrew the old name. What was the objection?
opts: The name duplicated a French appellation, and no imported name may appear on an American label
A variety name may not be printed on a wine made from a different variety
The variety had been dropped from the list of vines California permits growers to plant
The name was one producer's registered trademark, so no other winery could lawfully print it
exp: Once the identification was made the label was describing a grape that was not in the bottle, and long usage rescues nothing. Producers were given time to sell through their stock and then had to print the correct name. Several other borrowed names left American labels in the same period, for the same reason.

q: Two Bordeaux varieties share the word Sauvignon and a guest supposes that one must be a red version of the other. What is the actual link?
opts: Cabernet Sauvignon is a colour mutation of Sauvignon Blanc
Cabernet Sauvignon is a crossing of Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc
Sauvignon Blanc is a white-berried mutation of the Cabernet Sauvignon vine
There is no link at all; the shared word attached itself to unrelated vines
exp: The shared word records a parent. The crossing happened by chance in a Bordeaux vineyard, most probably in the seventeenth century, and the parents were identified only in the 1990s. Both are still widely grown, which is unusual and is what made the case straightforward to prove once the tools existed. A shared word in two grape names occasionally does mean something, and this is one of the rare occasions.

q: Across one list appear Muscadet, Muscadelle and Muscat, and a guest takes the three for variations on a single grape. Which reading is correct?
opts: All three are French names for one variety
All three name members of the Muscat family
Two of the three name grapes of the Muscat family, and the third names the Loire village they were first grown in
One is an appellation, one is a Bordeaux variety unrelated to the family, and only the third names that family
exp: The first is an appellation in the western Loire and no modern label prints it as a grape name; the second is a minor white of Bordeaux whose name is the only thing it shares with the aromatic family; the third covers a whole group of related aromatic vines. Three labels, three quite different kinds of word. Nothing but the first five letters connects them.

q: A section of an English wine list is headed Claret, and a guest goes looking for a grape of that name. What is the word actually doing?
opts: Naming red Bordeaux in English trade usage
Marking a Bordeaux wine above a set alcoholic strength
Standing as an old English name for Cabernet Sauvignon
Marking any wine built from two or more varieties
exp: It descends from clairet, the pale red the region shipped to England in the Middle Ages, and survived in English as a general word for the region's reds. It binds nobody to anything, which is why it also turns up as a fanciful name on bottles from other countries. A guest who asks for it wants red Bordeaux, or something built to resemble it.

q: A guest reads the word varietal on your list and takes it for a mark of quality. What does the word denote?
opts: A wine of better quality than a blend, since a single grape has nothing to hide behind
A wine from a single vineyard, small enough that one variety fills the whole of it
A wine made without any oak
A wine named after, and made principally from, one grape variety
exp: The word describes how a wine is labelled and nothing else, so a varietal wine can be superb or dismal and can still draw on many parcels and many sites. The opposite of a varietal wine is not a poor wine but a wine sold under a place name or a brand. A good many of the most expensive bottles in the world are not varietal wines at all.

q: Twenty countries stand side by side on one supermarket shelf, and most of the bottles can be compared at a glance because they print the same handful of words. Which labelling convention allows that?
opts: Protected designations of origin, which tie a name to one delimited place
Estate bottling statements, which say who grew the fruit and who bottled it
Vintage dating, which puts the year of the harvest on the front label
Varietal labelling, which puts the grape variety on the front
exp: A shopper who has learned six grape names can navigate a shelf drawn from a dozen countries, which is why the practice spread out of California through the New World and into the cheaper European tiers. A place-labelled bottle asks far more of its reader and repays it with far more information.

q: A grape name fills the front of a bottle and no region appears anywhere on it. What has that grape name said about where the wine grew?
opts: Nothing at all, since a variety name carries no origin with it
That the fruit was drawn from more than one country
That the fruit came from the variety's home region
That the wine was made outside Europe
exp: Varieties are planted on every wine-growing continent, so a name on its own places a wine nowhere. Rules elsewhere on the label still require an origin statement of some sort, and on the cheapest wines that can be as wide as a whole trading bloc. Variety and origin are two separate claims, made separately and checked separately.

q: A back label heads its list of grapes with a single French word that a guest mistakes for a quality term. Which word introduces the varieties?
opts: Millesime
Cuvee
Cru
Cepage
exp: Cepage is simply the French for grape variety, and a German label uses Rebsorte and an Italian one vitigno in the same place. Cru points at a vineyard or a ranking and millesime at the year, so the three words answer three quite different questions. Recognising which of them a line is answering is most of the work of reading an unfamiliar label.

q: An appellation permits one grape and one grape only, and the producer prints that grape's name on the front anyway. What is it doing there?
opts: Answering buyers who shop by variety, since the rules already settle what is in the bottle
Warning that a second variety is present as well
Satisfying a rule that the variety must always be stated once an appellation permits only one grape
Signalling that the wine comes from a single vineyard
exp: Naming the variety is an optional particular almost everywhere, so a producer adds it where the export market expects it and leaves it off where the appellation sells itself. It costs nothing and answers the first question a buyer trained on New World labels will ask. Optional does not mean unchecked, since a statement a producer chooses to make is still one the rules will hold him to.

q: A dozen countries with little else in common plant the same short list of grapes, in good part because those names are recognised on an export shelf. What are those grapes collectively called?
opts: International varieties
Crossings
Clonal selections
Indigenous varieties
exp: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc and Syrah travel further than any others, and a grower planting them buys instant recognition at the price of saying anything local. The reaction against that is the revival of indigenous varieties, whose names sell nothing on their own and have to be explained bottle by bottle. Both strategies are visible on any modern list.

q: No grape is named anywhere on a European red, and its producer has broken no rule at all. Why is the variety missing?
opts: The variety appears only on bottles intended for export
The blend changes from year to year, so it cannot be stated
European producers may not print a variety name on a front label
The appellation already settles which grapes may be used
exp: Where the rulebook fixes the grapes, naming them on the label adds nothing, since the place name carries that information for anybody who knows the rules, and centuries of labels were written for people who did. The information is assumed rather than hidden. Supplying it for a guest who has not got it is a good part of what a sommelier is for.

q: A by-the-glass list is arranged by grape, and one European bottle on it names no grape anywhere. Where should it be filed?
opts: It cannot honestly be listed by variety at all
Under its appellation, since no variety is stated
Under the variety its appellation requires
Under whichever variety the guest is most likely to expect
exp: The wine is made from that grape whether or not the label says so, and a list exists to help a guest choose rather than to reproduce a label word for word. Printing the appellation and the variety together is the usual solution and teaches the guest something on the way. What the heading claims has to be checked against the rulebook behind the name rather than against the label alone.

q: Told that a place name implies a grape, a guest concludes that any European label can be decoded that way. Where does the reasoning fail?
opts: Where the wine is white rather than red
Where the producer also owns vineyards in another appellation
Where an appellation permits several varieties at once
Where the appellation covers a very small area
exp: The name there fixes a style rather than a grape. Plenty of appellations run to a dozen permitted grapes or more, and two wines from one such name can be built quite differently and both comply. In those places the label tells you the rulebook was followed and only the producer's own literature tells you the blend. The single-variety appellation is the easy case rather than the general one.

q: One appellation makes a red and a white, and the two wines are not made from the same grape. What does a buyer need in order to read either label?
opts: The vintage, since the grapes alternate from year to year
The name of the company that bottled them
The variety the rules assign to each colour within that one name
The alcoholic strength of each of the two wines
exp: A single denomination frequently covers several colours, each with its own permitted varieties, its own ceiling on yield and sometimes its own ageing rules. The place is one word and the rulebook behind it runs to many pages. That is the practical reason a place-labelled bottle demands more of its reader than a varietal one does.

q: Vineyards in a European village were planted to whatever local practice required, and every buyer for miles knew what that was. What did that leave worth printing on the bottle?
opts: The place, because it was the only part that varied
The producer's trade, because few buyers could read
The grape, because buyers wanted it confirmed
The strength, because it varied most from year to year
exp: Where custom, and later law, settled the variety for everyone in the village, naming it would have been like printing the language a book is written in. What differed from bottle to bottle was whose land the wine came from and how good that land was. The convention has long outlived the conditions that produced it, which is why half the world now needs it explained.

q: A New World label prints a region on one line and a variety on the line beneath it. What is each of those two lines doing?
opts: The region carries the origin claim and the variety names the plant
Together the two form a single protected name
The region is decoration and only the variety is audited at all
The variety is decoration and only the region is regulated
exp: Both statements are audited, against different rules, and neither one depends on the other for its truth. The arrangement is what gives such labels their reputation for plain speaking, since the two questions a buyer asks are answered in two lines. A European bottle answers the first and leaves the second to the reader.
